title: There are wounds in families that money cannot heal.
paragraphs:
There are wounds in families that money cannot heal.
Titles cannot heal them.
Power cannot heal them.
Even anointing cannot heal them.
And one of the most devastating examples in all of Scripture is the relationship between David and Absalom.

David killed giants.
David defeated kingdoms.
David wrote psalms that still shake hearts thousands of years later.
But David could not fix his own son.
That reality terrifies many parents because deep down they understand something painful:
You can win battles in public while losing your children in private.

The tragedy of Absalom is not just rebellion.
It is unresolved pain slowly turning into destruction.
And Scripture gives us far more depth than most people realize.
The story begins long before Absalom rebelled.
It begins with David’s hidden compromises.
In Hebrew thought, sin was never viewed as isolated behavior. Sin created ripples. Corruption spread through households, generations, leadership, and relationships.
When David sinned with Bathsheba, the prophet Nathan warned him in 2 Samuel 12:10:
“The sword shall never depart from thine house.”
The Hebrew phrase is terrifying.

“לֹא־תָסוּר חֶרֶב מִבֵּיתְךָ”
“Lo tasur cherev mibbeitekha.”
Literally:
“The sword will not turn away from your house.”

This was not merely punishment.
It was consequence.

David received forgiveness from God.
But forgiven men still live with shattered outcomes from sinful decisions.
That truth is important because modern culture often treats grace as immunity from consequences.
Scripture never teaches that.
David’s household slowly began collapsing from the inside.
Then came Tamar.
Absalom’s sister.
David’s son Amnon raped her.
The Hebrew text in 2 Samuel 13 is emotionally brutal. Tamar tears her robe, puts ashes on her head, and cries openly in devastation.
But what breaks the story apart is David’s response.
Or rather…
His lack of response.
2 Samuel 13:21 says:
“But when king David heard of all these things, he was very wroth.”
That is all.
He was angry.
But he did nothing.
The Septuagint Greek tradition adds something powerful that many English readers miss:

“καὶ οὐκ ἐλύπησε τὸ πνεῦμα Αμνων”
“And he did not grieve the spirit of Amnon.”
Meaning David refused to confront him.
Why?

Many scholars believe David felt morally compromised after Bathsheba.
A guilty father often struggles to correct guilty children.

David had authority.
But his moral clarity had weakened.
And Absalom watched all of it.
This is where bitterness began mutating inside him.
The Hebrew word often associated with bitterness and root corruption is:

“שֹׁרֶשׁ” — shoresh
“root.”
Hebrews 12 later echoes this idea in Greek:

“ῥίζα πικρίας”
“rhiza pikrias”
“root of bitterness.”

Bitterness is never static.
It grows underground before it destroys things above ground.
Absalom waited two full years before acting.

Two years carrying rage.
Two years carrying humiliation.
Two years watching his father protect dysfunction.
Then he murdered Amnon.

Not impulsively.
Strategically.
And David again failed to deal with things correctly.
Absalom fled.
Eventually David allowed him back into Jerusalem…
But refused to see him.
Imagine that psychological contradiction.

Close enough to return.
Not close enough to restore.
2 Samuel 14:24:
“Let him turn to his own house, and let him not see my face.”
The Hebrew phrase:

“וּפָנַי לֹא יִרְאֶה”
“u’panai lo yir’eh”
“he shall not see my face.”
In ancient Hebrew culture, seeing the king’s face symbolized acceptance, restored relationship, covenant peace, and reconciliation.
David offered proximity without healing.
Many families still do this today.
People live in the same house while remaining emotionally exiled.
And this is where Absalom became dangerous.
Hurt people who remain unrestored often become manipulative people.
Absalom eventually stole the hearts of Israel.
Scripture says in 2 Samuel 15:6:
“So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.”
The Hebrew word for “stole” is:

“וַיְגַנֵּב” — vayegannev
“To steal secretly, deceive, carry away subtly.”
Absalom became externally charming while internally corrupted.
That combination is deadly.
People who never heal often learn how to perform.

Absalom stood at the gates greeting people before they reached the king.
He created emotional access where David had created emotional distance.
And this is one of the deepest lessons in the entire story:
Children often seek from strangers what they could not receive from wounded parents.
David could lead a nation…
But he could not emotionally reach Absalom anymore.
Not because David stopped loving him.
But because delayed obedience creates relational fractures that become harder and harder to repair.
Then came the devastating climax.
Absalom rebelled against his own father.
Civil war erupted.
And during battle, Absalom’s hair became caught in a tree.
There is symbolism there many overlook.
The very thing associated with his pride became part of his downfall.
2 Samuel 18 describes him suspended between heaven and earth.
Then Joab killed him.
When David heard the news, one of the most heartbreaking cries in all of Scripture exploded from him:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee…”
In Hebrew:

“בְּנִי אַבְשָׁלוֹם בְּנִי בְנִי”
“Beni Avshalom, beni beni…”
“My son Absalom, my son, my son…”
This is not kingly language.
This is shattered father language.
And the tragedy is this:

David loved Absalom deeply.
But love without righteous action failed to save him.
That sentence alone convicts many people.
Because affection is not the same as biblical leadership.

David avoided confrontation when it mattered most.
Avoided discipline.
Avoided restoration.
Avoided difficult truth.
And avoidance eventually became catastrophe.
The story also prophetically points toward Jesus Christ.
David cried:
“I wish I could die for my son.”
But David could not.
Jesus did.
This is where the Gospel enters the wreckage.
The greater Son of David accomplished what David never could.
Jesus stepped into rebellion, sin, shame, bitterness, and estrangement and actually died in our place.
The Greek of John 3:16 says:
“Οὕτως γὰρ ἠγάπησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν κόσμον…”
“For God so loved the world…”
The word “ἠγάπησεν” — ēgapēsen — speaks of sacrificial covenant love.
Not sentimental love.
Saving love.
Transforming love.

David’s love wept.
Jesus’ love bled.
That difference changes eternity.
And many people reading this are secretly carrying an “Absalom story.”

Maybe you were the wounded child.
Maybe you were the passive parent.
Maybe bitterness has been growing underground in your spirit for years.
Maybe unresolved pain has already started affecting your relationships, marriage, children, or faith.
But the Gospel still calls people out of hidden destruction.

Christ can heal what families could not.
Christ can restore what pride destroyed.
Christ can uproot bitterness before it becomes rebellion.
But healing requires truth.

Real repentance.
Real surrender.
Real humility.
Not image management.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending everything is okay.
David and Absalom teach us something terrifying:

Unhealed wounds do not disappear with time.
They mature.
And some people do not realize they are bleeding on everyone around them until entire relationships collapse.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.

And if this reminded you of someone struggling with bitterness, family pain, rebellion, father wounds, or spiritual distance from God, share this with them. Somebody is quietly falling apart behind a strong appearance.
Some wounds stay hidden until they start speaking through the people we become.
